extracted.intended_audience: computer scientists and mathematicians (students and authors) writing research and expository papers and articles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing, editing, and preparing mathematical/computer-science research and expository papers (titles, exposition, proofs, notation, interaction with editors, and typographic conventions). Aimed at producing readable, accurate, and audience-appropriate manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations — use and location
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotations to illustrate points; you may take quotations entirely out of context, quote yourself, or find someone famous to say something relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be creative in locating and using quotations (e.g., search on keywords in online texts to find suitable passages). Examples/antipatterns: quoting out of context can still be effective; desperate cases can quote unrelated passages that express the needed sentiment. Track attribution carefully (example: 'God is in the details' origin uncertain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and manage editorial changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect that journal editors will substantially edit manuscripts, sometimes rewriting many sentences and changing style and word choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate editing, review changes critically, and respond constructively. Request proofs (especially for technical material) and check them carefully: many typesetting/notation errors appear only at page-proof stage. Use direct negotiation (e.g., phone calls) when needed to correct technical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author–editor collaboration — insist on technical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should insist on correctness of technical notation and formatting when editors rework text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out introduced errors and demand corrections (examples: wrong symbol substitutions, parentheses/bracket misuse in formulas). For heavy technical material, request sight of proofs because typesetters unfamiliar with mathematics often introduce mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and accessibility — avoid unexplained jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Make exposition clear to the intended audience; excessive jargon indicates lack of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If editors introduce errors, that can reveal unclear exposition. For general-audience venues, remove jargon and simplify explanations to increase accessibility (SA edits removed jargon and made the paper suitable for a general readership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions and notation — be explicit and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose notational conventions deliberately (e.g., 'lg' for log base 2) and be prepared to defend them or adapt to journal norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that journals may change notation (e.g., 'lg' → 'log') with semantic consequences. Clarify numeric formatting choices (commas, spaces) for formulas vs text. If a convention is important, state it explicitly and check proofs to ensure it was preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and openings — get the reader's attention immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use snappy titles, arresting first sentences, and lucid initial paragraphs to hook readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong title and opening paragraph help readers decide to continue; fame of author can help but good craft matters (examples: 'Trisecting the Angle...' and provocative first sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-loading — tell readers upfront what you will do
rubrics_metrics.description: Get everything up front in plain English so readers can decide if they are interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the problem, main results, and contributions early. This increases readership (claim: can quintuple readership). Avoid hiding key statements deep in discursive text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make key results scannable
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers skim; make theorems and main results easy to find and understand at a glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize results (use boldface or similar emphasis), avoid heavy notation or cryptic abbreviations in theorem statements, and make statements self-contained so page-flippers can latch on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation and examples — use sparingly and purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide some motivation and examples, but do not overdo them; too many illustrative examples can lose their charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use motivating examples that build intuition and prepare the reader for the result. A few well-chosen examples are better than many trivial ones. Beware of gratuitous 'Consider the following...' constructions that signal left-field material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of style — 'chatty' exposition vs 'lean' proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a mixed style: be chatty and engaging in exposition around proofs, and 'lean and mean' in the proofs themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a personal voice: explain and motivate informally before a proof, present the formal proof tersely and rigorously (à la Rudin), then be chatty again afterward to discuss implications or intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format experimentation — choose formats that fit content
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider unconventional formats (e.g., dialogues, Q&A) when they serve exposition or engage readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialog formats have been effective (examples: Lamport's paper and Knuth's Surreal Numbers). Use format choices to convey feeling or intuition about the subject, but ensure they aid rather than obscure understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and terminology — choose clear, durable names
rubrics_metrics.description: Select terminology thoughtfully; names and terms can stick and influence future usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware you may later regret names if they are misleading. Community feedback can drive renaming (example: 'Polynomially-complete' → 'NP-complete'). If a term is important, consider community polling or established conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples/puzzles to build intuition before formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Present puzzles or motivating examples that let readers experience the problem and appreciate the algorithm/proof that follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing a theorem via a puzzle builds the 'right mental structures' for the reader. Even if the eventual algorithm is complex or inelegant, the example helps set expectations and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of detail — tailor proofs to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much detail to include in proofs based on the venue and audience; provide fuller exposition for expository journals and concision for technical audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two legitimate approaches exist: short, dense presentations that assume more from the reader versus longer, more explanatory treatments. Choose the approach appropriate to the publication (e.g., The MONTHLY favors exposition; Journal of Algorithms favors new/important results even if terse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic conventions and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear typographic conventions (fonts, code/logic fonts, consistent styling) to improve readability of formal material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: present logical formulas in typewriter font; ensure consistent use of brackets/parentheses. Good typographic choices reduce reader confusion and typesetter-induced errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and findability
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide useful indexing and consider how readers will search for material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexes matter for discoverability; anecdote: Sears advised searching whole catalogue if not in index. Ensure titles, abstracts, and keyphrases support findability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page layout and paragraph formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to visual layout details such as paragraph indentation and last-line lengths to avoid odd-looking pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust wording minimally to maintain visual consistency (example: ensure the last line of a paragraph is at least as long as the indentation on the following one), since weird breaks draw negative attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption writing and typesetting constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Write captions concisely and be prepared to adjust wording to fit typesetting rules where final line is right-aligned without extra space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may reword captions (often by removing words like 'the') to make line breaks fit; aim for concise captions and check final typeset proofs for caption layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-usage decisions — rely on evidence not prescriptivism
rubrics_metrics.description: Make usage decisions (e.g., sentence adverbs like 'hopefully') based on historical/dictionary evidence, not on ill-informed prescriptive attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of older citations and dictionary definitions supports legitimate uses of constructions such as 'hopefully' as a sentence adverb; ignore arbitrary prohibition that lacks linguistic evidence.
